steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting the BatVision dataset, a large real-world audio-visual dataset for research on sight and sound, audio-visual 3D scene understanding and robotic echolocation. Motivate why sound helps, why real data is missing, and briefly describe what the dataset contains.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Large-scale datasets and the new direction of listening to the environment
2. Lack of large real data for audio-visual 3D scene understanding; our echolocation motivation
3. Sound-augmented task performance
4. The BatVision Dataset: what and where
5. Outline of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- large-scale datasets propelled research: first static images, later videos; object detection to activity recognition
- sounds correlated with visual data provide info about action/context, often at marginal computational overhead
- new direction: listen to the environment for better task performance
- simulated room impulse response (RIR) datasets: sound vs. known space layouts; depth prediction, obstacle avoidance, driving towards alarm beyond line of sight
- predict 3D layouts from simulated chirps, like bats finding prey
- robots with echolocation: instant maps beyond surroundings without LiDAR/cameras; those fail in smoke and darkness

2. Missing real data
- some recorded RIR datasets within limitations; no large-scale real dataset for audio-visual 3D scene understanding for robots
- hinders domain adaptation from simulation, learning robustness to / exploiting real background sounds
- bats navigate and localize prey in flight with echolocation
- our earlier work: audible echoes of chirps for depth prediction
- need more real data in robotic scenarios to see how far this complements failing vision and extends beyond field of view
- -> BatVision Dataset: public, large-scale real data, complex scenes

3. Sound-augmented task performance
- sound arrives omnidirectional, rich info about space it crosses
- correlated with vision -> complementary when visual sensors fail
- cameras and LiDAR: occlusions, reflections, smoke; depth-from-stereo artifacts in low light, textureless objects
- audio-visual combination: one modality labels the other
- biomimicking echolocation improves 3D scene understanding
- such data sparse: complex setups, long sessions; small task-specific datasets; very few simple datasets for robotic echolocation

4. BatVision Dataset
- motivated by success of simulated datasets + lack of real data
- robot traversing real campus spaces; many materials, room shapes, objects (Figure 1)
- synchronized RGB-D images + echoes of chirps from forward facing speaker; like RIRs, infer room geometry; bat-like perception in darkness, smoke, fog
- UC Berkeley 52,220 instances, Mines Paris PSL 3,120 instances
- chirps 20 Hz to 20 kHz
- Intel Realsense on robot (Mines Paris), ZED camera (UC Berkeley)

5. Outline
- place among similar datasets, unique utility; collection process, data, depth prediction results
- BV1 = UC Berkeley, BV2 = Mines Paris

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale datasets have pushed research forward in past decades, first with static images and later with lots of videos, for tasks from object detection to activity recognition.

Sounds are correlated with the visual data of their source, and they give exploitable information about an action or context, often with only marginal computational overhead.

A new research direction is to listen to the environment to improve task performance. Simulated room impulse response (RIR) datasets let researchers study how sounds interact with known space layouts, for e.g. depth prediction, obstacle avoidance or driving towards an alarm beyond the line of sight. They have been used successfully to predict 3D layouts from simulated chirps, similar to how bats find their prey. Robots that master this echolocation could make instant maps beyond their immediate surroundings without LiDAR or cameras, which have limitations in smoke and darkness.

Some datasets provide recorded RIRs within limitations, but there is no large-scale real dataset to study audio-visual 3D scene understanding for robots. This makes domain adaptation from simulation harder, and also learning to be robust against real world background sounds or even to exploit them.

Bats can navigate and localize prey in flight using echolocation. We showed successfully how to adopt this for machine listening, using only audible echoes of chirps for depth prediction. To understand how far this method can complement failing vision sensors and even go beyond the field of view, we need more real data in typical robotic scenarios. So we present the BatVision Dataset, which provides publicly available large-scale real data of complex scenes for research on audio-visual 3D scene understanding and robotic echolocation.

Sound-augmented Task Performance.
- sound omnidirectional, rich info about space it crosses; correlated with vision -> complementary when visual sensors fail
- cameras/LiDAR: occlusions, reflections, smoke; depth-from-stereo artifacts in low light and textureless objects
- audio-visual combination, one modality labels the other; biomimicking echolocation helps 3D scene understanding
- data sparse (complex setups, long sessions) -> small task-specific datasets; very few simple ones for robotic echolocation

The BatVision Dataset.
- motivated by simulated datasets' success + lack of real data
- robot traversing real campus spaces; materials, room shapes, objects (Figure 1)
- synchronized RGB-D + echoes of chirps from forward facing speaker; infer room geometry like RIRs; darkness, smoke, fog
- UC Berkeley (52,220 instances), Mines Paris PSL (3,120 instances); chirps 20 Hz to 20 kHz; Intel Realsense on robot (Mines Paris), ZED camera (UC Berkeley)
- outline: related datasets, collection, data, depth prediction; BV1 = UC Berkeley, BV2 = Mines Paris

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale datasets have pushed research forward in past decades, first with static images and later with lots of videos, for tasks from object detection to activity recognition.

Sounds are correlated with the visual data of their source, and they give exploitable information about an action or context, often with only marginal computational overhead.

A new research direction is to listen to the environment to improve task performance. Simulated room impulse response (RIR) datasets let researchers study how sounds interact with known space layouts, for e.g. depth prediction, obstacle avoidance or driving towards an alarm beyond the line of sight. They have been used successfully to predict 3D layouts from simulated chirps, similar to how bats find their prey. Robots that master this echolocation could make instant maps beyond their immediate surroundings without LiDAR or cameras, which have limitations in smoke and darkness.

Some datasets provide recorded RIRs within limitations, but there is no large-scale real dataset to study audio-visual 3D scene understanding for robots. This makes domain adaptation from simulation harder, and also learning to be robust against real world background sounds or even to exploit them.

Bats can navigate and localize prey in flight using echolocation. We showed successfully how to adopt this for machine listening, using only audible echoes of chirps for depth prediction. To understand how far this method can complement failing vision sensors and even go beyond the field of view, we need more real data in typical robotic scenarios. So we present the BatVision Dataset, which provides publicly available large-scale real data of complex scenes for research on audio-visual 3D scene understanding and robotic echolocation.

Sound-augmented Task Performance. Sound arrives from all directions and gives rich information about the space it crosses. Because sound and vision are correlated, it can give complementary information when visual sensors fail. Cameras and LiDAR have problems with occlusions, reflections and smoke. Depth-from-stereo algorithms produce artifacts in low-light conditions and when objects have no texture. Combining audio-visual information can improve task performance, with one modality giving labels for the other. Biomimicking the echolocation principle can even improve 3D scene understanding using sound.

Audio-visual data that is suitable for these tasks is sparse, because real-world recordings need complex setups and long sessions. Because of this, researchers often create small datasets tailored to their own tasks. For research on robotic echolocation, only very few simple datasets exist.

The BatVision Dataset. Because simulated datasets have been successful and real data for robotic echolocation and audio-visual scene understanding is lacking, we recorded the real-life BatVision dataset. We provide large-scale recordings from a robot traversing real campus spaces, which cover a wide range of materials, room shapes and objects, shown in Figure 1. We provide synchronized RGB-D camera images and recorded echoes of chirp sounds sent out by a forward facing speaker. Like RIRs, the echoes can be used to infer the geometry of the room, so the robot can have bat-like perception even in darkness, smoke and fog.

The data was collected at UC Berkeley (52,220 instances) and Mines Paris PSL (3,120 instances). The emitted chirp signals range from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. RGB-D images were recorded with an Intel Realsense camera mounted on a robot (Mines Paris) and with a ZED camera (UC Berkeley).

In the following we place the BatVision dataset among similar datasets and argue why it is uniquely useful. Then we describe the collection process and the data, and show the performance of depth prediction methods trained on it. We will call the UC Berkeley data BV1 and the Mines Paris data BV2.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale datasets propelled research in past decades, providing first static images and later an abundance of videos for tasks from object detection to activity recognition.

Sounds, correlated with visual data from their source, provide exploitable information about an action or context, often at marginal computational overhead.

A novel research direction aims to listen to the environment for improved task performance. Simulated room impulse response (RIR) datasets allow researchers to investigate the interaction of sounds with known space layouts for e.g. depth prediction, obstacle avoidance or driving towards an alarm beyond the line of sight. They have been used successfully to predict 3D layouts from simulated chirps, similar to how bats find their prey. Robots mastering this echolocation could create instant maps beyond their immediate surroundings without LiDAR or cameras, overcoming their limitations in smoke [1] and darkness.

While some datasets provide recorded RIRs within limitations, no large-scale real dataset exists to investigate audio-visual 3D scene understanding for robots. This hinders domain adaptation from simulation, as well as learning to be robust against or even exploit real world background sounds.

Bats are capable of navigating and localizing prey in flight using echolocation. We showed successfully how to adopt this feat for machine listening, using only audible echoes of chirps for depth prediction [2,3]. To understand the extent to which this method can complement failing vision sensors and even extend beyond the field of view, more real data in typical robotic scenarios is needed. We therefore present the BatVision Dataset, providing publicly available large-scale real data of complex scenes for research on audio-visual 3D scene understanding and robotic echolocation.

Sound-augmented Task Performance. Sound arrives omnidirectionally and provides rich information about the space it crosses. Due to the correlation of sound and vision, it can provide complementary information when visual sensors fail. Cameras and LiDAR struggle with occlusions, reflections and smoke. Depth-from-stereo algorithms produce artifacts in low-light conditions and when objects lack texture. Combining audio-visual information can improve task performance, with one modality providing labels for the other [4,5]. Biomimicking the echolocation principle can even improve 3D scene understanding using sound [2,6,7].

Audio-visual data suitable for these tasks is sparse because real-world recordings require complex setups and long sessions [8,9,10]. Consequently, researchers often create small datasets tailored to their tasks [4,11]. For research on robotic echolocation, only very few simple datasets exist.

The BatVision Dataset. Motivated by the success of simulated datasets and the lack of real data for robotic echolocation and audio-visual scene understanding, we recorded the real-life BatVision dataset. We provide large-scale recordings from traversing real campus spaces with a robot, covering a wide range of materials, room shapes and objects, as shown in Figure 1. We provide synchronized RGB-D camera images and recorded echoes of chirp sounds emitted with a forward facing speaker. Similar to RIRs, echoes can be used to infer the geometry of the room, allowing the robot bat-like perception even in darkness, smoke and fog.

Data was collected at UC Berkeley (52,220 instances) and Mines Paris PSL (3,120 instances). Emitted chirp signals range between 20 Hz and 20 kHz. RGB-D images were recorded with an Intel Realsense camera mounted on a robot (Mines Paris) and a ZED camera (UC Berkeley).

In the following, we place the BatVision dataset among similar ones and argue its unique utility. We then detail the collection process and data, and showcase the performance of depth prediction methods trained on it. UC Berkeley data will be referred to as BV1 and Mines Paris data as BV2.

References:

[6] Ruohan Gao et al. “Visualechoes: Spatial image representation learning through echolocation” In Proceedings of ECCV , 2020
[7] Chenghao Zhang et al. “Stereo Depth Estimation with Echoes” In Computer Vision–ECCV 2022 Proceedings , 2022 Springer
